---
title: "Events"
---

The [sample-space construction](possibilities-and-events.qmd#outcomes-and-the-sample-space)
defined an outcome as one keyed row sampled uniformly from the 167-token
Turkish extract. Most linguistic questions do not ask which exact token was
sampled. They ask whether that token has a property. We represent such a
question by collecting all token outcomes that make its answer “yes.”

We define token-level events, construct their intersections, unions, and complements, and then distinguish an event excluded by the model from one that merely has not appeared in the extract.

An [**event**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html) is a subset of the sample space. Once a sigma-algebra $\mathcal F$ has been specified, the measurable events are exactly its members.

```{r}
#| label: load-events-data
library(ggplot2)

wh <- read.csv(
  "data/ud-turkish-boun/question-core-arguments.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
  fileEncoding = "UTF-8"
)
wh$outcome_id <- paste(wh$split, wh$sentence_id, wh$token_id, sep = ":")

stopifnot(nrow(wh) == 167L, !anyDuplicated(wh$outcome_id))

omega <- wh$outcome_id
N <- omega[wh$lemma == "ne"]
O <- omega[wh$dependency_relation == "obj"]
```

## Lemma and relation events

Let $N$ be the event that the sampled token's annotated lemma is *ne*, and let $O$ be the event that its annotated dependency relation is `obj`:

$$
N
\equiv
\{\omega\in\Omega:L(\omega)=\textit{ne}\},
$$

$$
O
\equiv
\{\omega\in\Omega:R(\omega)=\texttt{obj}\}.
$$

These definitions use properties of tokens to identify subsets of $\Omega$.

For instance, `train:pop:pop_1479:29` is the *Ne* token displayed on the
preceding page; its lemma is *ne* and its relation is `obj`, so it belongs to
$N\cap O$. The first displayed *kim* subject token belongs to neither $N$ nor
$O$. Membership is decided row by row before any event is counted.

## Intersection, union, and complement

The intersection contains tokens in both events:

$$
N\cap O
\equiv
\{\omega\in\Omega:\omega\in N\text{ and }\omega\in O\}.
$$

The union contains tokens in either event or both:

$$
N\cup O
\equiv
\{\omega\in\Omega:\omega\in N\text{ or }\omega\in O\}.
$$

The complement contains tokens outside an event:

$$
N^c
\equiv
\Omega\setminus N.
$$

```{r}
#| label: compute-token-events
N_and_O <- intersect(N, O)
N_or_O <- union(N, O)
not_N <- setdiff(omega, N)

event_sizes <- c(
  omega = length(omega),
  ne = length(N),
  object = length(O),
  ne_and_object = length(N_and_O),
  ne_or_object = length(N_or_O),
  not_ne = length(not_N)
)

stopifnot(
  event_sizes[["ne_or_object"]] ==
    event_sizes[["ne"]] + event_sizes[["object"]] -
    event_sizes[["ne_and_object"]],
  event_sizes[["ne"]] + event_sizes[["not_ne"]] ==
    event_sizes[["omega"]]
)

event_sizes
```

The code mirrors the notation exactly: `intersect(N, O)` computes $N\cap O$,
`union(N, O)` computes $N\cup O$, and `setdiff(omega, N)` computes
$\Omega\setminus N=N^c$. These functions return outcome identifiers, not
probabilities; `length()` counts the resulting event members.

The intersection contains `r length(N_and_O)` tokens. The union contains `r length(N_or_O)` tokens, which is smaller than the sum of the two event sizes because tokens in $N\cap O$ would otherwise be counted twice.

```{r}
#| label: plot-event-atoms
#| fig-cap: "Counts in the four nonoverlapping atoms formed by the *ne* and `obj` events."
atoms <- aggregate(
  outcome_id ~ ne_lemma + object,
  data = wh,
  FUN = length
)
names(atoms)[3] <- "tokens"
atoms$lemma_event <- ifelse(atoms$ne_lemma == 1, "ne", "other lemma")
atoms$relation_event <- ifelse(atoms$object == 1, "obj", "nsubj")

ggplot(atoms, aes(lemma_event, tokens, fill = relation_event)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge", color = "white") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(nsubj = "grey", obj = "steelblue")) +
  labs(x = "Lemma event", y = "Tokens", fill = "UD relation") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

## Membership and limiting events

For a particular token outcome $\omega_i$, either $\omega_i\in N$ or $\omega_i\notin N$. The realized outcome also determines whether $N$ and $O$ co-occur: both occur exactly when $\omega_i\in N\cap O$.

Two events delimit every event space. The impossible event contains no outcomes,

$$
\varnothing,
$$

whereas the certain event contains every outcome,

$$
\Omega.
$$

Every event satisfies

$$
\varnothing\subseteq E\subseteq\Omega.
$$

The event definitions are empirical in content but formal in structure. Their observed sizes come from the table; the set operations do not depend on those sizes.

Events turn linguistic properties into subsets of token outcomes. The [next page](event-spaces.qmd) asks which collections of these subsets can receive probabilities coherently.

## Check your understanding

1. Use the displayed event objects to compute $|N\setminus O|$ and interpret that event linguistically.
2. Verify in R that $N\cap O=O\cap N$ and $N\cup O=O\cup N$.
3. Use `wh` to define the event $K$ that the lemma is *kim*. Are $K$ and $N$ mutually exclusive in this token experiment?
4. Explain why $N^c$ means “retained tokens whose lemma is not *ne*,” not “all non-*ne* words in Turkish.”
5. A student reports `length(N) + length(O)` as the size of $N\cup O$. Which
   tokens have been counted twice?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. $|N\setminus O|=35$; these are retained *ne* tokens annotated `nsubj` rather than `obj`. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. R returns identical sets for `intersect(N, O)` and `intersect(O, N)`, and likewise for the two orders of `union()`, verifying commutativity. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. The *kim* event $K$ and the *ne* event $N$ are mutually exclusive because `intersect(K, N)` contains no token. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. $N^c$ is defined relative to the retained sample space $\Omega$, so it contains the 20 retained non-*ne* tokens rather than every non-*ne* word in Turkish. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
5. Every token in $N\cap O$, the *ne* objects, enters both addends and must be
   subtracted once.

</details>

Set operations give events their substantive interpretation: intersections
encode joint properties, unions encode inclusive alternatives, and complements
are always relative to the declared sample space. The [next
page](event-spaces.qmd) asks which collections of such events can receive
probabilities coherently.
